title: Saved by Grace, Made One in Christ
summary: Paul describes his readers' former condition: dead in trespasses and sins, following the ways of the world and the ruler of the power of the air, children of wrath. But God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ, raised them, and seated them with him, saving them by grace through faith, not by works. Then Paul turns to a second separation: Gentiles, once far from God's people and promises, have been brought near by Christ's blood, and Christ has broken down the wall between Jew and Gentile, making one new humanity and one holy temple where God dwells by his Spirit.
story: Chapter 1 ended with God's mighty power raising Christ from the dead and seating him above every power. Chapter 2 shows that the same power has been at work in believers: God has raised them with Christ and seated them with him. The chapter moves along two lines. The first (verses 1 to 10) is the story of every human being, Jew or Gentile, rescued from death by grace. The second (verses 11 to 22) is the story of the Gentiles in particular, once shut out from Israel's covenants and now made fellow citizens with God's people. Together they show that the gospel reconciles people both to God and to one another. Chapter 3 will explain this reconciliation as the mystery Paul was called to proclaim.
historical:
The dividing wall of hostility (v. 14) would have had a concrete meaning for anyone who knew the Jerusalem temple. Herod the Great's temple complex was surrounded by a large outer court that Gentiles could enter, separated from the inner courts by a stone barrier. Along that barrier stood notices in Greek and Latin warning foreigners not to go further on pain of death; the first-century Jewish historian Josephus describes them, and one complete Greek inscription of this kind was discovered in Jerusalem in 1871, with a fragment of another found in 1935. According to Acts 21:27-29, Paul was seized in the temple because some thought he had brought Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, past that barrier. Paul's image need not refer only to that wall, but it is hard to imagine a sharper picture of the separation Christ has removed.

If Paul wrote the letter, the temple was still standing and still in use; it was destroyed by the Romans in AD 70. Ephesians describes a new temple, built not of stone but of people, Jews and Gentiles together, in whom God dwells by his Spirit.
cultural:
In the ancient world, belonging mattered enormously. Cities distinguished citizens, who had rights and a share in civic life, from resident foreigners and strangers, who did not. Households distinguished family from outsiders. Paul uses exactly these categories: once the Gentile readers were alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers and foreigners, but now they are fellow citizens and members of God's household (vv. 12, 19).

The ruler of the power of the air (v. 2) reflects a widespread ancient belief that the air between earth and the heavens was inhabited by spirits. Paul uses that language to speak of the devil's influence over a world in rebellion against God. The cornerstone (v. 20) was the first and most important stone laid in a building, which set the line for the rest; some scholars think the word may instead refer to a capstone at the top of an arch. Either way Christ is the stone that holds the whole building together.
literary: The chapter is built on contrasts of before and after. In verses 1 to 10 the turn comes at verse 4 with “But because of His great love for us, God”: humanity dead, God rich in mercy. Paul uses three compound verbs meaning made alive with, raised up with, and seated with Christ (vv. 5-6), linking believers' destiny to Christ's own resurrection and exaltation. In verses 11 to 22 the same pattern appears: “remember that formerly” (v. 11) and “But now in Christ Jesus” (v. 13). Verse 17 echoes Isaiah 57:19, peace to those far and near. The closing verses pile up building language (foundation, cornerstone, fitted together, temple, dwelling place), bringing the chapter to rest on the image of God's house.

outline.t: Made alive, raised, and seated with Christ
Saved by grace through faith, created for good works
Gentiles once far away, now brought near
Christ our peace: one new humanity
Fellow citizens and a holy temple

doctrines.note: Humanity apart from God is described as dead, not merely weak: following the world, under the influence of the evil one, driven by the desires of the flesh, and by nature children of wrath. Paul includes himself and his fellow Jews (v. 3).
Salvation is by grace through faith, the gift of God, not from ourselves and not by works (vv. 8-9). Yet it produces good works, which God has prepared for his people to walk in (v. 10).

The church is one new humanity made from Jew and Gentile, a household and a temple built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone. Its unity across the deepest division of the ancient world is part of the gospel itself.
Christ reconciles both Jew and Gentile to God in one body through the cross (v. 16). His death deals with the hostility between people and God and, because of that, the hostility between people.

words.note: Charis, grace: God's free, undeserved favor. It is the key word of verses 5 to 8. Grace is the source of salvation, faith is the way it is received, and the whole is God's gift. In Greek culture charis could describe a benefactor's generosity, which created obligations of gratitude; in Paul, God's grace goes to those who were his enemies.

Poiema, workmanship or thing made. It gives English the word poem, though the Greek simply means something crafted. Believers are God's handiwork, newly created in Christ for good works (v. 10). The word is also used in Romans 1:20 for the created world.

Mesotoichon, dividing wall, a word found only here in the New Testament. Christ has torn down the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile. Many readers connect it with the barrier in the Jerusalem temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts.

Akrogoniaios, cornerstone, the foundational stone that set the alignment of a building. The word comes from the Greek version of Isaiah 28:16, which 1 Peter 2:6 also applies to Christ. The whole structure of God's people depends on him.

christ: The chapter shows Christ as the place where both great separations are healed. Believers are made alive with him, raised with him, and seated with him in the heavenly realms (vv. 5-6); what God did for Christ at Easter he does for those united to Christ. And Christ himself is our peace (v. 14): by his blood Gentiles are brought near, in his flesh the wall of hostility comes down, and through the cross Jew and Gentile are reconciled to God in one body. Through him both have access to the Father by one Spirit (v. 18). He is the cornerstone of a new temple, and the temple is his people.

hard.q: What does it mean that Christ abolished “the law of commandments and decrees” (2:15)?
hard.a:
Paul's words could be read as saying the Old Testament law has simply been done away with, which seems to sit uneasily with Jesus's statement that he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17). Interpreters handle this in several ways. Some think Paul means the law as a body of commandments that separated Jews from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws, and purity rules, which no longer mark the boundary of God's people. Others take the phrase more broadly: the law as a whole, as a covenant arrangement and a condition of standing before God, has been brought to its end in Christ, though its moral vision is fulfilled in the life of the Spirit (compare Romans 13:8-10). Still others distinguish between moral, ceremonial, and civil parts of the law, a distinction with roots in the early church and developed by later Christian theologians, and see the ceremonial law as what is abolished here.

What the text makes clear is the result: the law no longer functions as a wall between Jew and Gentile, and Christ has created one new people in himself. Paul does not say the moral will of God has changed; the following chapters are full of moral instruction.

questions: Paul describes life apart from God as being dead, not just sick. How does that change the way you think about grace?
Verse 10 says we are created for good works that God prepared in advance. How do grace and good works fit together in your own understanding?
What walls divide people in your church or community, and what would it look like for Christ's peace to take them down?
